    Third-Party Code

    This page documents every third-party library and external service the Digital Logbook depends on, and — more importantly — why each one was chosen. Our policy is to lean on well-maintained, permissively licensed libraries for solved problems (authentication primitives, email, build tooling) while hand-writing everything that is core to the product (the REST API, business logic, database schema and UI components).

    Every package below is declared in package.json (per workspace) and its license was verified from the installed package.json on disk.

    How we evaluate dependencies

    Before adding a library we check:

    1. Fit — does it solve a problem we would otherwise hand-roll poorly (crypto, date handling, bundling)?
    2. Maintenance — is it actively maintained and widely adopted?
    3. License — permissive (MIT / BSD / Apache-2.0) so it is safe for a university project; no copyleft surprises.
    4. Size — is the dependency worth its footprint on the bundle?

    Backend runtime dependencies

    Package License What it does Why we chose it
    express ^5.2 MIT HTTP framework for the REST API Minimal and unopinionated — the course requires a hand-written API, and Express gives us routing/middleware without generating code or hiding the API behind heavy abstractions. v5 has native async error handling.
    @prisma/client ^7.9 Apache-2.0 Type-safe database access The generated client turns every query into TypeScript-checked code — schema drift becomes a compile error, not a runtime crash. Schema-as-code also gives us reviewable migrations.
    @prisma/adapter-pg ^7.9 Apache-2.0 Driver adapter for PostgreSQL Prisma's driver-adapter pattern lets us bring our own pg connection pool, which is the recommended way to talk to Neon's serverless Postgres over a pooled connection string.
    pg ^8.23 MIT PostgreSQL wire-protocol driver Required by the Prisma adapter; a mature, battle-tested driver.
    zod ^4.4 MIT Schema validation One validation library shared by frontend and backend through @logbook/shared — the same Zod schema validates the register form in React and the request body on the server. Single source of truth, no drift.
    jsonwebtoken ^9.0 MIT Signs and verifies JWTs Stateless auth: the server issues a signed token and verifies it on every request without a session store. The de-facto standard library for HS256 JWTs in Node.
    bcryptjs ^3.0 BSD-3-Clause Password hashing Pure-JavaScript bcrypt. We chose it over the native bcrypt package specifically because it needs no compilation — no node-gyp/native-module issues on teammates' Windows laptops. Same algorithm, identical hashes.
    otplib ^13.5 MIT TOTP two-factor authentication (RFC 6238) Implements the same standard that Google Authenticator / Authy use, so users can use any authenticator app. Actively maintained successor to speakeasy.
    qrcode ^1.5 MIT QR code generation Renders the otpauth:// provisioning URI as a QR data URL so users can scan it with their phone camera instead of typing a base32 secret.
    nodemailer ^9.0 MIT-0 Transactional email over SMTP Works with any SMTP provider — we send through Gmail with an app password — so there is no vendor lock-in and it works in local development without an API account.
    cors ^2.8 MIT Cross-Origin Resource Sharing middleware The frontend (Vite dev server on :5173, deployed frontend on Cloudflare Pages) calls the backend on a different origin; cors handles the preflight/OPTIONS dance correctly.
    dotenv ^17.4 BSD-2-Clause Loads .env into process.env Twelve-factor configuration: secrets (DB URL, JWT secret, Gmail credentials) stay out of the codebase.
    resend ^6.20 MIT Email API client Installed but not yet wired up. Being evaluated for the Sprint 2 external-API integration requirement as a possible replacement for raw SMTP sending.

    Frontend dependencies

    Package License What it does Why we chose it
    react ^19.2 + react-dom MIT UI component runtime Component model fits the app (many reusable cards, forms, modals); the team knows it best; huge ecosystem.
    react-router-dom ^7.18 MIT Client-side routing declarative route tree with route guards — our ProtectedRoute wrapper redirects unauthenticated visitors to /login.
    axios ^1.19 MIT HTTP client Chosen over fetch for its request/response interceptors: one interceptor attaches the JWT to every call, another catches 401s (expired session) and redirects to login. Automatic JSON parsing is a bonus.
    lucide-react ^1.31 ISC Icon library Consistent, stroke-based icon set that tree-shakes — we import only the icons each page uses, so the cost per icon is tiny.
    zod ^4.4 MIT Client-side form validation Same schemas as the backend (see above) — the register/login forms validate with the exact rules the server will enforce.

    Shared package (@logbook/shared)

    Package License Purpose
    zod ^4.4 MIT The validation library the shared auth schemas are written in. This package is the reason the frontend and backend can never disagree about what a valid registration looks like.

    Development tooling (devDependencies)

    Package License Where Why
    typescript ^6.0 Apache-2.0 everywhere Type safety across the monorepo; tsc --noEmit typechecks CI and every commit.
    vite ^8.2 MIT frontend Instant HMR in development and optimised, hashed-asset production builds.
    @vitejs/plugin-react ^6.0 MIT frontend Fast Refresh + JSX transform for React under Vite.
    tailwindcss ^4.3 + postcss + autoprefixer MIT frontend Utility-first CSS keeps styling inside the components; v4 compiles away unused styles. Responsive prefixes (sm:, lg:) are how the app meets the responsive-design requirement.
    tsx ^4.23 MIT backend Runs TypeScript directly in npm run dev with watch mode — no separate build step while developing the API.
    vitest ^4.1 MIT backend Test runner with native TypeScript/ESM support and a Jest-compatible API; runs our 78 integration tests. See Testing.
    supertest ^7.2 MIT backend Lets tests fire real HTTP requests at the actual Express app (through the real auth middleware and Zod validation), rather than calling handlers with fake request objects.
    eslint ^10 + typescript-eslint ^8 MIT backend Lints the backend with TypeScript-aware rules.
    oxlint ^1.75 MIT frontend Rust-based linter — fast enough to run on every save.

    External services

    Service Role Why
    Neon Hosted PostgreSQL Serverless Postgres with autoscaling and a generous free tier; branching would let us copy the database for experiments. Chosen over self-hosting so the team never maintains a DB server.
    Gmail SMTP Transactional email Verification and password-reset emails are sent through a Gmail account with an app password — zero cost, no signup friction, and it works locally.
    Render Backend hosting Deploys the Express API from main with a free tier that suits a student project.
    Cloudflare Pages Frontend + docs hosting Global CDN for the built React app and this MkDocs documentation site.
    Gitea (sdp.ms.wits.ac.za) Version control, CI, issue tracker University-hosted Git server; runs the CI workflow on every push and hosts the bug tracker we use for all defects.

    Licensing summary

    All dependencies use permissive licenses — MIT, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC, Apache-2.0 or MIT-0. There is no copyleft (GPL/AGPL) code in the dependency tree, so the project's own licensing is unaffected.
